stories.title: Boy, 2, killed in Limerick hit-and-run named locally
stories.summary: A two-year-old boy, who died in a hit-and-run incident in Co Limerick, has been named locally as Peter Mulcaire. The boy, who is understood to be from Abbeycourt, Rathkeale, was pronounced dead after being struck by a car near his home yesterday afternoon. He was taken to University Hospital Limerick by a family member for treatment of serious injuries. The boy was subsequently pronounced dead and gardaí have said that a post-mortem examination will take place in due course. The incident occurred in the town, which is located around 30km southwest of Limerick city, shortly after 3.50pm. Prayers for Peter Mulcaire will be said at Sunday masses across St Mary's Parish, Rathkeale and the Diocese of Limerick this morning.

He was taken by a family member to University Hospital Limerick (UHL) for treatment of serious injuries, where he was subsequently pronounced dead. A man in his 30s was arrested at a different location under suspicion of driving under the influence of an intoxicant. He was questioned at a garda station in Limerick and has been released, pending analysis of an evidential sample. A post-mortem examination will be conducted at UHL by the State Pathologist tomorrow.

stories.title: Trump to meet President at Áras during visit next weekend
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump is to meet President Catherine Connolly at Áras an Uachtaráin during his planned visit to Ireland next weekend. He is likely to arrive in Dublin early on the morning of Saturday 12 September, before travelling on Marine One helicopter to the Phoenix Park for meetings with Ms Connolly and Taoiseach Micheál Martin. Mr Trump will spend Saturday night at his golf resort in Doonbeg for the Irish Open tournament. The US president's sons Eric and Don Jr will attend the event in Doonbeg next week. It is understood the brothers will not be travelling with the president. While a bilateral meeting with Mr Martin at Farmleigh House has long been expected, there had been doubt over whether the US President would meet President Connolly.

stories.title: Lost its Shein? Why the fashion giant's value has slumped
stories.summary: When Shein raised funds privately in 2022, few would have predicted it to be a high-water mark for the Chinese fast-fashion giant. Back then the company's blistering growth made it seem like the inevitable future market leader in global fashion – with its $100 billion valuation that year perhaps even seeming modest to some. But after aborted attempts to float shares in both New York and London, the company this week debuted in Hong Kong – securing a price-tag of less than $27 billion. That’s despite the fact that it is now a much bigger company than it was back in 2022. That year, it’s thought to have had sales of around $27 billion globally. In terms of profit, it was likely making somewhere in the region of $700m. Compare that to last year, when the company had revenues of more than $41.8 billion, and a profit of more than $2 billion – and that far-lower valuation may not make much sense.

stories.title: Panama Canal begins reducing crossings due to El Niño
stories.summary: The Panama Canal has begun to reduce the number of ships passing through due to a drought caused by the El Niño weather phenomenon. The Panama Canal Authority said low water levels in the two artificial lakes that feed the canal forced it to act. The number of vessels allowed through the waterway connecting the Atlantic and Pacific oceans will be progressively lowered from 36 per day to 32 by mid-September. Panama has declared a nationwide emergency over El Niño, a weather pattern developing over the Pacific Ocean that is triggering worldwide changes in winds, atmospheric pressure and rainfall and pushing up global temperatures. This year's El Niño is expected to be the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago. It has not yet reached its peak, but Central America is already in the throes of a severe drought, prompting Honduras and El Salvador to also declare emergencies.

stories.title: No stone left unturned as Wicklow look to harness power
stories.summary: In the end, it was a very simple equation. Oisín McConville wanted to know that Wicklow still wanted him, Wicklow wanted to know if McConville still wanted them. The first part was an easy yes, but the second was potentially trickier. After Wicklow's brilliant Tailteann Cup triumph, the Armagh man’s stock was never higher. A cluster of county and high-profile club positions awaited him, if he so wished. Wicklow chairman Damien Byrne was also conscious to give his manager as much space as he wanted. McConville's mother Margaret – herself so revered in the Orchard County – died just over a month ago. In the end when the time was right to chat, it was an easy yes for McConville too. Earlier this week it was confirmed that the 2002 All-Ireland winner would take charge of the Garden County for a fifth season. Rarely will Wicklow football look forward to a new season with such enthusiasm. There was the All-Ireland B title in 1992 on the mouth of Christmas under a still-in-his-20s Niall Rennick, the side getting the better of Antrim in Navan.

stories.title: Kildare's Rattigan embracing football's new era
stories.summary: After playing a full season of inter-county football under the LGFA's new playing rule enhancements, Aoife Rattigan is enjoying doing the same with her club Cappagh as they work their way through the highly-competitive Kildare intermediate football championship. Having initially trialled them during the Lidl National Football League and the Higher Education colleges competitions, the LGFA fully approved 12 new rules for their games at a Special Congress in April of this year. Whereas six of these regulations mirror the changes brought into the men’s game – such as the two-point scoring arc, the 'three up’ rule and the ‘solo and go’ – the rest were focused more so on the current rules of the LGFA. Rattigan thoroughly enjoyed playing under these new rules for the Lilywhites and continued to embrace them by kicking no fewer than three two-pointers in Cappagh’s opening round intermediate group stage win at home to Confey on 11 August. Although Cappagh as a team weren't as familiar with the rule enhancements as those who had been operating on the inter-county scene, Rattigan believes her club colleagues have quickly come to terms with the way the game is now being played. "I loved playing the new rules all year with Kildare, but at the start it took us a while to get used to them," she said.

stories.title: Liverpool sporting director Hughes leaves role
stories.summary: Liverpool's sporting director Richard Hughes has stepped down after just over two years in the job. Hughes, who has long been linked with Saudi Arabian club Al Hilal, oversaw the largest spending spree in the club’s history with the £450 million spent last summer on the likes of British record transfer Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz and Hugo Ekitike, supplemented by a further £250m in the most recent window. That saw the arrivals of France international Bradley Barcola, in a deal potentially rising to £123m, defender Jeremy Jacquet, Spain winger Victor Munoz and goalkeeper Lucca Brughmanns, although the latter will not join until next season. It is believed Hughes made his decision earlier this year, following Michael Edwards’ departure as owners Fenway Sports Group’s chief executive of football, but due to the work he had already undertaken – particularly in relation to Barcola – it was agreed he would see out the summer window. It is also understood at no point was permission sought or offered for Hughes to work for any other club during this period and the club are entirely satisfied this agreement was honoured. Fenway Sports Group president Mike Gordon, who will lead the process to find a replacement, said: "Richard joined us at the start of a period of change, embracing that responsibility by leading our football operations department and overseeing recruitment while also providing valuable support to our coaching staff.

stories.title: Refreshed Van der Flier ready for World Cup year
stories.summary: Leinster and Ireland flanker Josh van der Flier knows that nothing is won in early September, but that doesn't mean that the 2027 Rugby World Cup escapes the imagination ahead of the start of the 2026/27 season. Speaking at the launch of the IRFU’s new men’s and women’s national team jerseys at the Guinness Open Gate Brewery this week, the 33-year-old was in fine form, which could be attributed to a healthy body and mind. "(I’m) feeling fit as well and getting back into a bit of pre-season stuff and ready for a big few months." This optimistic outlook will come as soothing words to head coach Andy Farrell, who prepares his 12-month plan where all roads hopefully lead to a World Cup final in Sydney on Saturday, 13 November. Van der Flier was part of the two most recent touring squads to Japan in 2019 and France in 2023, where both Irish efforts were ended by the All Blacks. There is a feeling of now or never ahead of the next edition however, but van der Flier insists that he is taking the coming months one at a time. "It's always tempting to start thinking of those (major tournaments), but it's obviously like how rugby goes, it tends to be week-to-week and you've got to look after your pre-season first," he said.

stories.title: Something for the Weekend: Pauline Scanlon's cultural picks
stories.summary: Pauline Scanlon is one of Ireland's most distinctive voices, an artist deeply rooted in tradition yet constantly pushing its boundaries. A West Kerry native, her singing carries the weight of old songs while speaking powerfully to the present day. From her acclaimed debut Red Colour Sun to her work with LUMIERE, John Spillane, Dónal Lunny Damien Dempsey, Sinéad O’Connor and The Whileaways, Scanlon has built a career of remarkable collaborations and solo performances. She's recently been named TG4 Singer of the Year, to be presented at the Gradam Ceoil Awards in Limerick on September 13th. Gaza, directed by Garry Keane and Andrew McConnell. I've seen Gaza numerous times over the last number of years, often at Palestinian events, and it sears through to the heart every single time. What I find so powerful about the film is its refusal to offer a reductive portrayal of life in Gaza. Instead, it shows us its complexity: the humour, music, family, work, love, frustration, beauty and ordinary human ambition that exist alongside the brutality of life under blockade. As it was first released in 2019, watching it now carries an almost unbearable weight, but that insistence on the fullness and complexity of life is what makes the film so beautiful and affecting. I’ve had two records on repeat this summer. Child Ballads by Anaïs Mitchell and Jefferson Hamer is a collection of songs I love, sung with the most exquisite harmonies. There is a simplicity and intimacy to the whole record that really draws me in, and I’ve found myself returning to it again and again. The other is An Sionnach Dubh by Dàibhidh Stiùbhard from Co. Tyrone. Dàibhidh is, for me, one of the most beautiful traditional singers of his generation. He is such an accomplished singer, with a gorgeous repertoire and a real depth to his singing. As someone who loves traditional song, it is always exciting to hear a singer with that combination of ability, sensitivity and a great store of songs.

stories.title: Hugh Jackman delighted to have Irish damp in his bones
stories.summary: Backed by Northern Ireland Screen, The Death of Robin Hood is a dark retelling of the outlaw legend that sees the aged Robin (Jackman) trying to come to terms with what he has done while a prioress (Jodie Comer) shows him the path to a better life. Among the many stunning locations in the film from writer-director Michael Sarnoski (Pig, A Quiet Place: Day One) are Silent Valley Reservoir and Tollymore Forest Park in Co Down, Murlough Bay and White Park Bay, Co Antrim, and the Rock of Cashel, Co Tipperary. "I knew as I was shooting that this was a gift that I would... Hopefully, I'll get it back, but I may never get back, so I made the most of every moment. "Our last day of shooting at the Rock of Cashel was something I'll never forget. It was, like, 16 degrees and sunny that day... It was incredible." Jackman's only other trip across the Irish Sea was when he brought his The Man. The Music. The Show. tour to Dublin's 3Arena in May 2019. "I had this weird rule from drama school days when I did Brian Friel's Translations and we learned all about the history," he recounted. "And, of course, for every Australian, Ireland, it feels like a brother."

stories.summary: "Generally speaking, winter is very expensive," says Pope, explaining that heating and lighting our homes in the colder, darker months adds up. stories.title: Under-18 e-scooter ban could be in place by end of month
stories.summary:
Minister for Transport Darragh O'Brien has said a ban on the use of e-scooters by under 18s could now be introduced by the end of this month or early next month, after he received permission from Europe to proceed with the plans. The State had been advised that it needed to wait three months before the ban could be introduced, due to European rules, but Minister O'Brien received confirmation this afternoon that the European Commission had waived this waiting period, after accepting the case to have an urgent adoption of the measures. Minister O'Brien has welcomed the decision, saying he will now move to draft the necessary regulations, with a view to increasing the minimum age for e-scooter use from 16 to 18 by late September or early October.

Regulations to make helmets and high-visibility clothing mandatory for e-scooter use come into effect from tomorrow. Those in breach of the regulations face a fixed charge notice of €100. From 2 October fees for detention and storage of seized e-scooters will be doubled, rising to €80 for detention and the first day of storage and €30 for each additional day or storage. In the coming weeks fixed Charge Notices will be increased to €100 for e-scooter offences.

stories.title: Volkswagen flags 50,000 more job cuts across car group
stories.summary: Volkswagen shares hit an 11-week high after the supervisory board of Europe's largest automaker last night struck an ambitious turnaround agreement that put the focus on sweeping job cuts and averted a clash between major stakeholders. The deal on the biggest restructuring in the group's 89-year history includes a further 50,000 job cuts, bringing the total agreed to 100,000, and leaves open the future of four of its German plants. Volkswagen, like most of its European peers, is under pressure from painful tariffs in the US, falling sales in former cash cow China and aggressive Asian rivals entering the stagnant European market. All these factors have gnawed at the group's operating margin, which stood at 3.8% in the first half, down from 7.9% in 2022, its peak over the past decade. Shareholders and analysts expressed relief that Volkswagen - with a workforce of more than 650,000, a complex structure and powerful stakeholder groups - is still able to make far-reaching decisions in times of crisis. Ingo Speich of Volkswagen shareholder Deka Investment called the agreement a breakthrough: "Does this mean Volkswagen is out of the woods? Definitely not. Now comes the hard part: execution."

stories.title: Death toll in Cyprus ferry disaster rises to 13
stories.summary: Rescuers recovered another body today from a ferry disaster off Cyprus last week, raising the death toll to 13, while 15 people remain missing, officials said. The FiloJet ferry was carrying 267 people when it capsized shortly after departing from the port of Kyrenia on the northern coast of the divided island around midday on Sunday. Round-the-clock search and rescue operations have continued since the accident. The latest recovery brought the number of confirmed deaths to 13, according to authorities in the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), a breakaway state recognised only by Ankara. "With the recovery of another body, the number of people who lost their lives in the accident has risen to 13, while the number of missing persons is now 15," TRNC Prime Minister Unal Ustel said. Authorities said the wreck of the ferry had been located at a depth of 554 metres off Kyrenia.

stories.title: Knockout KO'd - Tyrone continue to go against the grain
stories.summary: Quiz question - name the two counties that still employ a straight knockout format in their senior men's football championship? You should get halfway there given the fame attached with Tyrone’s continued decision to ignore changing times - and the much-cited fact that no club has retained the title since Carrickmore all the way back in 2005. The action throws in tonight with the meeting of Ardboe and Edendork while Loughmacrory will be hoping to end that back-to-back hex when they meet Dungannon on Saturday, but the fact of the matter is that if they’re not good enough then their title defence will be over at about 9pm this evening. The other county who still employs knockout football is less obvious, probably the last footballing county to come to mind. The Kilkenny senior championship is run off on a knockout format - the league determining where a team starts in the championship - with Mullinavat getting the better of Tullogher-Rosbercon back in early May. The fact that the final was held so early in the season speaks volumes for where it stands in a ferociously hurling-dominated county, so it's truly the Red Hand County where the last bastion remains unconquered. Niall Gartland, a Tyrone-based journalist with the Ulster Herald, has covered approximately 30 club championship games a season for the last decade. He believes the knockout format is not a lifetime guarantee but, likewise, he sees no appetite currently for change.

stories.title: Pat's v Bohs too close to call in FAI Cup quarter-final
stories.summary: Second and third place in the SSE Airtricity Men's Premier Division face off today in an exciting Club Orange FAI Cup quarter-final contest. Both teams have put up a fight to Shamrock Rovers, but with just a few games left, time may be running out for either team to win a miraculous league title. All eyes are on the cup. In the pick of the round, Bohemians make the short trip to Inchicore to face St Patrick's Athletic in Richmond Park, a trip that the Gypsies may have to get used to. Between the Bohs men’s and women’s teams there are seven games left in Dalymount Park in their respective leagues. The men also have a friendly against Bohemians Praha 1905, and their future is yet to be decided in the FAI Cup. After some farewell concerts, that will be it for the historic ground. Dalymount Park, as we know it, will be knocked down to make way for a brand new stadium. It was reported in June that Bohs were negotiating an agreement to play alongside their rivals Pat's for the next two seasons at least in Richmond Park.

stories.title: Leinster to return to Aviva for Munster clash in October
stories.summary: Leinster have confirmed their United Rugby Championship clash with Munster on the October Bank Holiday weekend will be played at Aviva Stadium. Leinster are going back to the RDS - now rebranded as Laya Arena - this season after the stadium's two-year redevelopment. They will play their first competitive game of the campaign there against Cardiff on 10 October. However the province will then make a quick return to Lansdowne Road, where they played most of their home matches last season. It's been confirmed the inter-pro derby against Munster will take place at the Aviva on Saturday, 24 October, 6pm kick-off. Last year the fixture took place at Croke Park, with Munster running out 31-14 winners in front of just under 52,000 fans.

stories.title: A House In Winter by Emily Hourican - read an extract
stories.summary: We present an extract from A House in Winter, the new novel from Emily Hourican. Set in January 1965, A House in Winter tells the story of the visit of Princess Margaret and Lord Snowden to his sister's home in Abbeyleix, Ireland, when they faced local opposition and IRA petrol bomb attacks that confined them, without electricity, for 48 fraught hours. As well as the conflict outside the walls, there's plenty within, with Margaret's difficult mother in law gleefully contributing to her disintegrating marriage. Meanwhile in the nearby village local woman Cait has struggles of her own, unable to escape family responsibilities and small town life. Both Margaret and Cait are trapped by their circumstances... 'Here, Your Highness, here!' they call, holding up cameras like babies to be admired. ‘This way!’ M rolls the window down as the car slows and the gates are opened, pulled apart by two men in cloth caps. She leans out to wave graciously. Beside her, Tony sighs. ‘I wish you wouldn’t,’ he says. ‘You’ll ruin this place. Corrupt it so that it becomes just like England – a nation of eager corgis waiting for the royal whistle.’ He laughs at his own joke, his lips parting in that toothy smile that makes him look by turns boy and wolf.

stories.summary: When Donald Trump last visited this country, Leo Varadkar was Taoiseach. They met in Shannon and the opening moments of their private meeting were dominated by an unlikely topic. At the time, the US president was having a social media spat with the actress Bette Midler. The former taoiseach recalls trying to "steer him off" that subject and on to more serious matters before the cameras came in. Indeed, in a recent interview with Colette Fitzpatrick, Mr Varadkar offered this searing insight into Donald Trump. "While he is an intelligent man, and nobody should underestimate him, he's not knowledgeable. "So, it's a very strange combination of somebody who's quite bright, manipulative, knows how to push buttons, [and] knows how to get people on side.

stories.summary: Tributes have been paid to "wonderful young boy" Eoin Doyle, who died after a train hit a car near Ballyhaunis, Co Mayo, on Thursday night. Eoin, who was 12 years old, and his father were travelling in the car when the collision occurred at a user-operated level crossing at Kiltybo, shortly before 9pm. His father was taken to hospital by ambulance for treatment. His injuries are described as not life-threatening. Eoin was a sixth-class pupil in Cloonfad National School and a much-loved member of local sport clubs. In a statement, the school's principal Shane Morgan said Eoin was a "friendly and kind child". "He was a talented artist and athlete, who loved music and a smile was never far from his face.

stories.title: Byrne confident of EU budget deal under Irish presidency
stories.summary: Minister for European Affairs Thomas Byrne has said he is "absolutely confident" that agreement can be reached on the next long-term EU budget before Ireland's Presidency of the EU concludes at the end of the year. European Affairs Ministers are meeting in Dublin today and tomorrow as talks on the next long-term EU budget reach a critical stage. One of the key aim's of Ireland's EU Presidency is to agree the budget, known as the multiannual financial framework (MFF), before the end of the year. However, several countries, including Germany, want to rein in spending. Speaking as he arrived at Dublin Castle for the meeting of the General Affairs Council, Mr Byrne stressed the urgency of the negotiations. "I'm absolutely confident we can achieve this by the end of the year because I think we need to, and the reason we need to is because we need to have the funds in place by the 1 January 2028.

stories.title: Oil heads for weekly gain as US-Iran fighting resumes
stories.summary: Oil prices were on course to gain more than 6% for the week as the US and Iran resumed military exchanges in the seventh month of their conflict, while US diesel prices hit a record high. Brent crude futures were up 6.1% for the week and US West Texas Intermediate crude futures had gained 8.3%. On the day Brent was flat at $95.54 a barrel by early evening, while WTI was down 0.6%, at $90.78. The rally in oil prices combined with a much steeper increase in fuel prices has pushed inflation and government borrowing costs higher around the world and intensified warnings that the global economy might be heading for a hard landing. "All sectors of the economy are affected by diesel. This is one of the reasons why the government bond yields in the US are so high, it's the expectation that inflation will continue to go up," said Claudio Galimberti, chief economist at Rystad Energy. Average US diesel prices hit record highs as renewed US-Iran hostilities and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries increased supply disruptions.

stories.title: Mistrial declared in Clancy murder trial, jury discharged
stories.summary: A judge declared a mistrial in the high-profile case of an American woman who killed her three young children. Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict in the case of Lindsay Clancy and an appeals court rejected a last-minute bid by the defence to have a juror replaced. After seven days of deliberations, the 12-member Massachusetts jury was unable to reach a unified decision, as required in criminal proceedings in the United States. Eleven jurors were in favour of finding the 36-year-old Ms Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity, but they were opposed by a single member. "At this point, I'm going to declare that the jury is deadlocked, and I'm going to declare a mistrial," Judge William Sullivan said. Prosecutors must decide now whether to try the case again with a new jury.

stories.title: Dunlevy and Kelly retain their World Championship crown
stories.summary: Katie-George Dunlevy and pilot Linda Kelly retained their Women's B individual time trial world title in Huntsville on Saturday, leading an Irish gold and silver double as Sinead Greenan and pilot Alice Sharpe claimed silver on their World Championship debut. Dunlevy and Kelly completed the 29.2 km course in 36:55.48 to secure their fourth consecutive World Championship time trial title. Greenan and Sharpe followed in 37:28.08, finishing 32.60 seconds behind their teammates and 20.71 seconds ahead of Great Britain's bronze medallists Sophie Unwin and Jenny Holl. Dunlevy said: "It's absolutely unbelievable, very surreal and a huge relief. I felt pressure going into the race, but to deliver the ride and come away with a fourth time trial title is the stuff of dreams. "When you stand on the podium, all the work and sacrifices feel worthwhile. To have Sinead and Alice there as well makes it even more special." Kelly added: "The conditions were brutal, like a furnace. We settled into the first four kilometres and then started to build while managing the heat over two laps.
